source.title: The Effects of Mild Over-parameterization on the Optimization Landscape of Shallow ReLU Neural Networks
source.authors: Itay Safran; Gilad Yehudai; Ohad Shamir

record.file_problem: Full text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that affects the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes whether mild over-parameterization removes non-global minima in a two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem. Its theorem and experiments examine the effect of splitting neurons on minima, a different method and outcome measure from gradient-descent success rates.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the prior Safran and Shamir (2017) experiments on how often gradient descent encounters local minima, but those are not this paper's results. Its own experiment is for n=k; the split-neuron result is a theorem, not a measured gradient-descent success rate.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes landscape geometry and checks assumptions for neuron-splitting theorems. It does not measure whether extra width reduces gradient descent's frequency of reaching spurious minima from standard initialization, as V2 specifies. The reported width-dependent success rates belong to Safran and Shamir, not this study.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate as a possible explanation. The authors conditionally prove that neuron splitting turns existing non-global minima into saddles and empirically validate the technical conditions at found minima. They do not prove that wider networks lack new spurious minima or measure improved gradient-descent success rates.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies population squared loss for a shallow ReLU teacher-student network with Gaussian inputs and orthogonal unit teacher vectors. It analyzes neuron splitting and Hessian geometry, rather than measuring the V2 version's gradient-descent frequency across width settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The splitting guarantee assumes n ≤ k and Σᵢ ‖wᵢ‖ ≤ k; the authors note their analysis does not address new local minima that may form when n>k.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the norm-sum condition and n ≤ k, at least one neuron at a non-global minimum can be split to produce a saddle. All found minima satisfied the bound, and every tested H′ᵢ,ᵢ had a negative eigenvalue, implying that any neuron at those minima could be split into a saddle.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding a neuron through splitting can destabilize existing non-global minima in Gaussian-input ReLU teacher-student population objectives.

fits_no_version.finding: Exact parameterization gives locally strongly convex global minima, whereas over-parameterization removes local convexity, one-point strong convexity, and the PL condition. These results do not establish worse optimization success.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mild over-parameterization changes local geometry around global minima without preserving standard convexity conditions.

record.problems: The theorem's guarantee depends on a norm-sum condition; the authors do not prove it holds for all minima. The experiment checks found minima only at n=k and reports floating-point Hessian eigenvalue checks. The paper does not measure gradient-descent success rates after adding neurons.

untested.parts: Training classification error in convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, including corrupted labels.
Failure frequencies as teacher and student grow together, and their reduction with one or two extra student neurons under gradient descent from standard initialization.
Depth-related training degradation and its prevention through identity shortcuts or special training recipes.
Effects of initialization on training speed and trainable depth.
Loss and curvature dynamics relative to learning-rate stability thresholds.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparison with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The conditions on splitting are qualifications of a related geometric result, not scope limitations demonstrated for V2. Accordingly, no V2 verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR training error, random or corrupted labels, model size, optimizer, and training duration.

The paper does not measure gradient-descent frequencies of reaching spurious minima across teacher and student widths, or compare students with one or two extra neurons over widths 6 to 20. It studies a theorem about splitting neurons at non-global minima and empirically checks its technical assumptions at n=k.
Depth, shortcut connections, and training error in deep networks.
Initialization effects on training speed or trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability and loss or curvature dynamics.
Batch normalization and training speed or stability.

rows.subject: population objective F(w₁ⁿ) in Eq. (2)
rows.size_stated: student has n neurons; teacher has k neurons; theorem assumes n ≤ k
rows.operation_detail: Split a neuron at a non-global minimum into two neurons with the same direction and weights summing to the original neuron.
rows.measure: Whether the resulting critical point is a saddle point.
rows.baseline: The original point is a non-global minimum.
rows.value: The split point is a saddle point for all α ∈ (0,1).
rows.note: The theorem also states that at α ∈ {0,1}, the resulting point is not a local minimum. The result depends on the stated norm-sum condition.
rows.check: Theorem 8 guarantees that there exists a neuron whose splitting produces a saddle, under n ≤ k and the norm-sum bound; it does not guarantee this for an arbitrary neuron. This geometric result does not establish gradient-descent success rates after increasing width.

rows.subject: population objective F(w₁ⁿ) in Eq. (2)
rows.operation_detail: Check the norm-sum condition at gradient-descent-converged local minima.
rows.measure: Whether found local minima satisfy Σᵢ ‖wᵢ‖ ≤ k.
rows.value: All local minima found in the experiment satisfy this bound.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the reported experiment; this checks a technical assumption for Theorem 8, rather than measuring how often gradient descent reaches a global minimum.
rows.check: The norm-sum check is accurately reported but cannot establish V2's optimization-frequency effect. The experimental conditions omit 100 additional instantiations initialized with norm-sum roughly 2k².

rows.subject: population objective F(w₁ⁿ) in Eq. (2)
rows.operation_detail: Check the eigenvalues of each diagonal Hessian block component H′ᵢ,ᵢ at found local minima.

conditions.value: local minima found in the experiment

rows.measure: Whether each H′ᵢ,ᵢ has a negative eigenvalue.
rows.value: All block components for all minima found have a negative eigenvalue.
rows.note: The authors state this implies by Theorem 9 that splitting any neuron at any found minimum gives a saddle for α ∈ (0,1).
rows.check: The negative eigenvalues of H′ᵢ,ᵢ support the conditional splitting argument, not a measured reduction in gradient-descent failures. These are components of diagonal Hessian blocks; the full Hessians at the found minima had positive minimum eigenvalues.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Non-global minima satisfying the theorem's norm-sum condition
reader_labels.reason: Splitting a neuron turns the non-global minimum into a saddle for every α ∈ (0,1), under the stated condition (R1). The experiment reports the condition held at all found minima and each block had a negative eigenvalue (R2, R3).
